anchors.fact: New Orleans "was a Brandy Julep town" before the Civil War. In the decades after it the city "became much more Americanized", and an 1885 *Times-Democrat* interview had a bartender calling "brandy drinking in New Orleans… a thing of the past": whisky had "displaced it" (*Imbibe!* pdf 182). F9
anchors.meaning: The city's own drink was replaced by the newcomer's. The split is a change in what the city drank, told through the drinks, never through groups of people. It's 1860s–1885, about fifty years before the glass: never a live quarrel at the bar (C2).

anchors.fact: Walter Bergeron (1889–1947), then head bartender at the Monteleone Hotel, who "had worked at the bar before Prohibition and returned upon Repeal" (Oxford VIEUX CARRÉ, pdf 2102). F2
anchors.meaning: Someone with standing behind the city's bar. His own background and side aren't on record (C1). Say "the Monteleone's bar", never "the Carousel Bar" (C11). He's never Victor "Trader Vic" Bergeron (C8).

anchors.fact: He created the Vieux Carré "in the 1930s" (Oxford pdf 2102; *Joy* pdf 402). The 1937 recipe: ⅓ jigger each of rye whiskey, cognac brandy and Italian vermouth, with ½ tsp Bénédictine and a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura (Arthur 1937, 1984 reprint, archive.org OCR highlight). Oxford's modern spec: 30 ml each, 5 ml Bénédictine, 2 dashes each bitters; *Proper* p. 255: ¾ oz each. F3, F5, F6, F10
anchors.meaning: **Our reading** (signposted): the whiskey the city had taken up and the brandy it used to drink, poured at the same measure in one glass, neither cut below the other. It's **three** equal parts (vermouth too), never "half and half" (C4). Whether "full strength" or "the same measure" is Wren's call; "same measure" is the literal page. No reason for the pairing is on record (C7 revised); the drink's motive is the next row but one.

anchors.fact: "named for the French Quarter"; it "translates as 'old square'" (Oxford pdf 2102; *Joy* pdf 403). F4
anchors.meaning: The glass carries the old quarter's name. **Who chose it isn't on record** (C3): "it carries the old quarter's name", never "he named it". Our reading: the newcomer's spirit sits under the old city's name.

anchors.fact: Arthur 1937: Bergeron "takes special pride in mixing" it; "He originated it, he says, to do honor to the famed Vieux Carré, that part of New Orleans where the antique…" (archive.org OCR highlight of the 1984 reprint, matched in Pearce 2017). F12
anchors.meaning: His reason for the drink, in his words as Arthur relays them: to honour the old quarter. Tell it with the channel ("he told the man who first printed it" or "he said"). It gives **no** reason for putting the two spirits together: that stays "I like to think".

anchors.fact: Its recipe "first appeared in print in 1937" (Oxford pdf 2102, citing Stanley Clisby Arthur). F3

anchors.meaning: One clause at most (Wren's guard: Ciro's Manhattan is the Magnetic Leader's).

anchors.fact: Oxford: "typically served on the rocks", over fresh ice in a large rocks glass; "serving it up makes for a lovely presentation" (pdf 2102). F5
anchors.meaning: Both serves are on the page. Tomás's choice. Never "the way Bergeron served it" (C13).

anchors.fact: Cardamom on both the Grain wheel (p. 127) and the Grape wheel (p. 131) of the *Flavor Matrix*, rendered (F14). Steep scaled from *Codex* p. 288 (10 g/750 ml, ~12 h, room temperature; p. 95 on vermouth-strength liquids) (F15).
anchors.meaning: Our addition, said as ours: the shared part of the glass (the vermouth) changes, and neither spirit does. Scope: "the grain behind the rye and the grape behind the cognac", never "rye and cognac pair with cardamom". Never Bergeron's.

anchors.fact: Peychaud's and Angostura are both in the 1937 recipe (F6).
anchors.meaning: Name them as ingredients only. The pairing of both bitters is also O'Reilly's Sazerac (*Imbibe!* pdf 182): no Sazerac (C9).

cocktail.closingLine: Put the cardamom in the vermouth, never in either spirit. Next time you cross over, bring all of yourself.
cocktail.glassware: large rocks glass (about 300 ml), one large ice cube
method: The night before, put about 3 g of whole green cardamom pods (roughly 15) into 250 ml of sweet vermouth in a clean jar. Leave it at room temperature for about 12 hours, then strain it back into its bottle and keep it in the fridge. It's enough for eight drinks.
Pour the rye and the cognac into a mixing glass or jar, just as they come from the bottle.
Add the cardamom vermouth, the Bénédictine and both bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Put one large ice cube in the rocks glass and strain the drink over it.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

cocktail.tagline: Everyone wants you on their side. You keep ending up on both.

reading.epigraph: A city gave up brandy for whiskey. Years later, one glass poured both.
whoYouAre: A family stops speaking over a seating plan. A team splits down the middle over who did the work. Two neighbours each want you to say the other one's wrong. Everyone waits to see which table you'll sit at. You go and sit with the people who expected you not to, and you have whatever they're having.

You don't do it with a speech. You've never won anyone round with an argument, and you don't try. You just turn up on their ground and mean it. From outside it can look like sitting on the fence. It isn't. You have a side, and you know your own mind. The hardest question you get doesn't come from the other side. It comes from your own: whose side are you on? What you fear is being made to choose, and the day a row stops being a row and becomes the way things are. Because of you, nobody has to pick a table. Both halves end up in one room, and neither had to give itself up to get there.
yours: Before the American Civil War, New Orleans was a brandy town. Its juleps were made with brandy, and that was how the city drank. Then the city changed. By 1885, a bartender was telling a New Orleans newspaper that brandy drinking there was over, and that whiskey had taken its place. The city drank it in whiskey cocktails and in the new Manhattan.

By the 1930s, the Hotel Monteleone's head bartender was Walter Bergeron. He'd worked that bar before Prohibition and returned when it ended. The drink he created there became the hotel's signature. It's a Manhattan at heart, but where a Manhattan has whiskey, his has two spirits: rye whiskey and French cognac. They go in at equal measures, level with the sweet vermouth, plus two different bitters and a touch of a herbal liqueur from France, Bénédictine. Its name is the old quarter's: Vieux Carré, "old square".

He said he made it to honour the old quarter. Why he put those two spirits side by side, he didn't say. But I like to think it's the city's whole story in a single drink: the brandy it drank first and the whiskey it turned to, together in one glass, neither poured a drop less than the other. That's what you do. When people split, you don't rule on which half was right. You bring both in, at the same weight, and you call it by a name everyone already shares.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Vieux Carré, a renowned New Orleans classic, with the proportions of its first printed recipe: rye, cognac and sweet vermouth in three equal measures, none cut back for another. I didn't change either spirit. I steeped the vermouth overnight with green cardamom, as a nod to the ground the two sides share: of the three measures, the vermouth is the one that belongs to neither, and cardamom goes with both the grain behind the rye and the grape behind the cognac. It's stirred, rich and deep, with the rye's spice and the cognac's softer fruit each as clear as the other, and the cardamom warm in the vermouth between them.

One thing, though. When you go over to the other side, you tend to leave a little of yourself at the door, so they feel safe. Your own side notices, and that's where the question comes from. Don't pour less of yourself. It was never your quietness they trusted. It's that you came as you are and stayed. And when your own side asks again, you'll have your answer: both, and still me.
